one_line: Hands-on workshop: trace a Claude financial-analyst agent in Phoenix, read failures, write code and LLM-judge evals, validate judges against human labels, run experiments, and gate CI on them.
summary: Laurie Voss (Arize) walks through a full eval loop for a deliberately flawed financial-analyst agent built on the Claude Agent SDK, using Arize Phoenix for tracing and evals. The agent runs a research turn and a writing turn, and the speaker shows how auto-instrumented traces expose failures like writing to disk in unattended mode, invented numbers, and a non-actionable report. He stresses reading traces by hand first (open coding, then axial coding) so the eval categories come from real failures rather than guesses. He then layers three eval types: a code check that the ticker appears in the report, built-in Phoenix judges (correctness, which was the wrong question, and faithfulness, which worked), and a custom five-part "actionability" judge. The judge is validated against his own human labels using a dev/test split with precision and recall, and the talk ends with a model upgrade (Haiku 4.5 to 5.5) measured as an experiment, plus pass^k and CI gating with vitest. The main takeaway is that evals only help once you pick the right question, check the judge, and treat the eval prompts as code.

key_ideas.idea: Traces are the logs and evals are the tests run over them
key_ideas.detail: Each agent step (LLM call, tool call, nested agent turn) is a span with input, output, latency, tokens, and sometimes cost. Evals score those spans, so you can grade the output without adding logging by hand when using auto-instrumentation.

key_ideas.idea: Confidently wrong failures are the dangerous ones in agents
key_ideas.detail: Failures can start early and cascade. The example is a Tesla report that is well formatted but about an 18th-century inventor, so format and tone checks all pass. Agents can also be smarter than the rules: a tau-bench airline agent upgraded a user to first class to get around a seat rule, which a rigid test would mark as a failure.

key_ideas.idea: Read traces before writing any eval, then categorize
key_ideas.detail: Write free-text notes per trace first (open coding), then group them into categories (axial coding). Engineers tend to guess categories in advance and get them too narrow or wrong. Prioritize failure categories by frequency times severity, so rare but severe failures still rank high.

key_ideas.idea: Choosing the right eval matters more than tuning it
key_ideas.detail: The built-in correctness judge failed all 16 reports because it judges against its own training knowledge, so it could not verify fresh stock data. Faithfulness, which checks the report against the search results the agent actually saw, produced useful explanations. The question the judge asks has to be one it can answer with the context you give it.

key_ideas.idea: An LLM judge needs a five-part rubric, and examples can hurt as well as help
key_ideas.detail: The parts are role/context, specific criteria taken from error analysis, XML-tagged data, optional labeled examples, and constrained output via tool-call choices. Examples can cause overfitting, so test the judge with and without them. Changing one wrapper (XML tags) flipped many verdicts with the same data, so treat eval prompts as versioned code.

key_ideas.idea: Validate the judge as a classifier against human labels, with a held-out test split
key_ideas.detail: Label your own traces against the same criteria, then split by sorted span ID (every fourth example to test) so splits are stable across runs. Measure precision and recall, and favor recall for gating because a false alarm is cheaper than a missed failure. Tuning the rubric on dev data improved dev agreement from 12/12 to 11/12 while breaking one test case, which is why the held-out split matters.

key_ideas.idea: The bar for a judge is beating human-human agreement, not perfect agreement
key_ideas.detail: Cohen's kappa between expert annotators on this kind of task is often around 0.2 to 0.3, so a judge does not need to match you 100% of the time. Failures should also look fair when you read them; if a human reads a failure and says it looks fine, the eval is probably wrong.

key_ideas.idea: Use pass^k rather than pass@k for agents you care about
key_ideas.detail: pass@k rises with more tries (it succeeds at least once). pass^k asks whether every run succeeds, which matters for a financial analyst where one bad recommendation is a serious problem. Non-determinism means one run per example can mislead in either direction.

key_ideas.idea: A model upgrade can look like a win while hiding a new failure mode
key_ideas.detail: Haiku 5.5 was more consistent and its faithfulness improved more than threefold, but it chose 'hold' in 41 of 45 calls. Consistency was achieved by becoming overly conservative, and the eval exposed that problem only because it was measured. Cost rose about fourfold, which is a separate trade-off to weigh.

key_ideas.idea: Split evals into guardrails and north stars, then gate CI on the right kind
key_ideas.detail: Guardrails (like mentioning the correct ticker) block release on any failure. North stars (like an actionable recommendation) use an average threshold because a single LLM judge verdict is noisy. Capability evals that reliably pass become regression evals in CI.

techniques.name: Deterministic code eval with structured input
techniques.how: Pull the top-level spans via a parent-null query, read the JSON input for the requested tickers, and check each appears in the output. The score and label explain which ticker is missing. Anything that gives the same answer for the same input can be a code eval, including DB or API checks.
techniques.when: When the requirement is objective (required fields, mentioned entities, length limits, banned phrases) and you need it to run free and fast in milliseconds.

techniques.name: Faithfulness judge with full retrieval context
techniques.how: Pass the user input, the agent output, and the actual search results and notes the agent saw as context. Keep the judge's context consistent with what the agent had. Early versions flagged real numbers as fabricated because the judge was missing the raw search results.
techniques.when: When checking whether a generated answer is grounded in the sources an agent retrieved.

techniques.name: Five-part LLM judge prompt with constrained labels
techniques.how: Give the judge a role and context, specific criteria derived from error analysis, data wrapped in XML tags with template variables, optional labeled examples marked as examples, and output constrained via tool-call choices (for example actionable or not actionable). Run each dimension as its own evaluator.
techniques.when: When the requirement needs judgment about meaning (is this recommendation actionable, is this tone right) and you want a score plus an explanation.

techniques.name: Judge hygiene: different-family, stronger judge, suppressed tracing
techniques.how: Use a judge more capable than the agent being graded, ideally from a different provider to avoid same-model preference. Suppress tracing on the judge so its own calls do not pollute the agent's traces. Swap the order of options in pairwise tests to reduce position bias.
techniques.when: Whenever you run an LLM judge, especially with the same model family as the agent.

techniques.name: Open coding then axial coding of traces, with a coding agent
techniques.how: Write plain-language notes per trace first, then group the notes into categories. Use a Phoenix plugin or skill so a coding agent can scan traces, count categories, and write them back as annotations. Still manually read a sample, because the agent may miss categories you care about.
techniques.when: Before writing any eval, to discover the failure modes that actually occur in your traces.

techniques.name: Golden dataset with dev/test split by stable ID
techniques.how: Label traces by hand against the same criteria the judge uses. Sort examples by span ID and place every fourth one into a test split; the rest are dev. Tune only on dev, and check the test split once to confirm the judge generalizes. Add new production failures to the golden set over time.
techniques.when: When you need to know if a judge is trustworthy, and before changing its rubric.

techniques.name: Run experiments on the failing subset only
techniques.how: Turn the traces that failed a given eval into a Phoenix dataset. Run the experiment (agent task plus the relevant evaluators) against that dataset after each prompt change, rather than the whole suite each time.
techniques.when: When iterating on a prompt to fix a specific failure, to keep the eval loop fast and cheap.

techniques.name: pass^k reporting for nondeterministic agents
techniques.how: Run each example k times and report the rate at which all k runs pass, alongside pass@k. Use pass^k as the release metric when a single failure is costly.
techniques.when: For agents whose wrong answers are costly (financial advice, support refunds), where you need reliability rather than an occasional success.

techniques.name: Vitest-based eval suite gated in CI
techniques.how: Write each eval as a normal test case using a describe/test per query. Gate hard on guardrail evals (must pass) and on an average threshold for judge-based evals (such as at least 0.8). Run the Phoenix server as a service container in GitHub Actions. Print a scorecard with explanations on failure.
techniques.when: To stop regressions from shipping, once a capability eval is reliably passing and becomes a regression eval.

techniques.name: Eval-driven development
techniques.how: Write the eval before the feature so 'done' has a measurable definition, then iterate on the agent until the eval passes.
techniques.when: When starting a new agent capability with clear, checkable requirements.

numbers.claim: Code-eval run over 16 reports completed almost instantly: 15 passed, 2 failed (missing Tesla, missing Amazon) on the ticker-mention check
Built-in correctness judge marked 0 of 16 reports correct; 7 of 16 explanations complained the judge could not verify fresh data
Built-in faithfulness judge marked 14 of 16 reports unfaithful, with explanations that pointed at specific unsupported claims
13 of 16 writing turns tried to save a file to disk, which the built-in tool-selection judge mostly accepted as reasonable given the ambiguous prompt
Actionability split on the base run: 5 of 16 reports actionable, 11 not
Judge agreement with the human on 16 reports: 15/16 with examples in the rubric, 16/16 without examples in one of two configurations (across three runs)
Dev split of 12 reports reached 12/12 agreement with the human; a single added sentence broke one dev case (11/12) and one test case
With a 75/25 split on 16 golden labels, the test set is only 4 items, so the speaker says you need about 100 labels for a reliable test split
Human expert inter-annotator agreement (Cohen's kappa) on this kind of task is often around 0.2 to 0.3
Anthropic's Opus 4.5 scored 42% on CoreBench before test fixes; after fixing ambiguous and wrong tests the score reached about 95%
To halve error bars on accuracy, roughly quadruple examples; going from 25 to 100 is the speaker's suggested minimum jump
Experiment progress after prompt changes: actionability went from 5/16 to 48/48 on the run shown, while faithfulness only moved from 2/16 to 3/48
Haiku 4.5 to 5.5 upgrade: faithfulness improved more than 3x (still poor), cost rose about 4x, and 41 of 45 calls chose 'hold'
Full 15-query batch takes about 3 to 4 minutes at 5 concurrent runs; a 3-repetition experiment takes about 13 minutes
A Tesla report claimed 116% analyst consensus by adding two search results from different data sets

hot_takes: 'Looks good to me' is not a test suite, and three manual tries is not evidence.
Confidently wrong output is worse than obviously wrong output, and it is what agent evals most need to catch.
Choosing the right eval beats tuning it; a built-in correctness judge asked the wrong question and was useless here.
Your LLM judge does not need to agree with you 100% of the time; it needs to beat human-to-human agreement, which is often low.
Use a judge from a different provider than the agent to avoid same-model preference bias.
Grade outcomes, not the path the agent took; agents will find creative solutions you did not anticipate.
Don't build a god-evaluator that checks everything in one prompt; split evals by dimension.
Temperature is the least useful hyperparameter for agents, and modern models have stopped letting you set it.
Product managers, support, and sales should define what good looks like; the engineer should not do it alone.
Pick and tune your eval rubric by reading traces yourself first, not by starting from a list of checks you guessed in advance.
Being told to tip the model $100 in prompts is an 'allegedly helpful' trick, not something to rely on.

relevance.why: The talk's dev/test golden-set split, precision/recall on judge verdicts, and pass^k reporting are directly reusable for MemoryMesh's RAGAS evals and for SkillForge's open question about skill-worthiness signals.
relevance.action: Add a stable (span-ID-sorted) dev/test split and a judge-vs-human precision/recall report to MemoryMesh's RAGAS faithfulness evals before trusting their scores.

relevance.why: The speaker warns that the Claude Agent SDK runs the same engine as Claude Code, so user settings, tools, and skills leak into headless runs, causing non-determinism ('harness leakage'); ProsHarness wraps Claude Code, so it has the same risk.
relevance.action: Make ProsHarness headless or eval runs hermetic by isolating them from the user's ~/.claude settings and skills, and check for permission-asking in unattended mode.

relevance.why: The five-part judge rubric, judge-versus-human validation, and error-analysis-before-evals workflow are a concrete method for any LLM-judged eval we write, and the warning about judges with confident but wrong explanations applies directly to our cheap-model pipelines.
relevance.action: Before adding any LLM-judge eval (entity resolution, context-engineering checks), write a five-part rubric, label 20 to 50 examples by hand, and measure judge agreement on a held-out split; compare a stronger judge model against Haiku as the grader.
